case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. J. R. F.
key_cases.holding: Without resolving how far the juvenile code authorizes such orders, the court vacated an order requiring a father to make his other, non-ward children available for visitation with his ward, holding the record inadequate because ORS 419B.090(4) makes parental due process rights part of the construction and application of every provision of ORS chapter 419B.
key_cases.relevance: Bounds what a juvenile court may order a parent to do under a dependency case plan: whatever statutory authority exists is limited by the parent's right to direct the upbringing of children who are not wards.
key_cases.quote: the due process rights of parents are always implicated in the construction and application of the provisions of ORS chapter 419B

key_cases.case_name: State ex rel Dept. of Human Services v. Rardin
key_cases.holding: Reversing a termination judgment, the court held that because ORS 419B.504 permits termination only on grounds of present unfitness, the statute assumes parents can change, and a father whose earlier conduct had changed genuinely and lastingly could not be found unfit for failing to present an agency-satisfactory reintegration plan.
key_cases.relevance: Establishes that what the statute measures is the parent's actual change of conduct, not the parent's history or a failure to produce the reintegration plan the agency wanted.
key_cases.quote: the legislature assumes that parents can change their conduct and that, if the change is both genuine and lasting, the state may not terminate their parental rights for unfitness

key_cases.case_name: State ex rel Dept. of Human Services v. Smith
key_cases.holding: Reversing two terminations, the court held that DHS may not condition return of a child on compliance with service demands untethered to statutory unfitness, and that every fact supporting termination must be proved to a high probability.
key_cases.relevance: Defines the outer bound of court-ordered service plans — the conditions exacted of a parent must bear on statutory unfitness, not on the agency's preferred standard of parenting.
key_cases.quote: Under that standard, the court must find that the evidence establishes that the truth of the facts asserted is highly probable.

key_cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. Y. B.
key_cases.holding: The court held that a juvenile court's 'sufficient progress' determination under ORS 419B.476(2)(a) is a legal conclusion reviewed for legal error, not a finding of fact, and affirmed the change of plan to guardianship.
key_cases.relevance: Measures a parent's progress on the ordered service plan as a question of law rather than an unreviewable fact finding.
key_cases.quote: Thus, the text of the statute suggests that the juvenile court's determinations of "reasonable efforts" and "sufficient progress" are legal conclusions.

key_cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. C. H.
key_cases.holding: The court held that reasonable efforts under ORS 419B.476 are assessed on the totality of the circumstances, including whether services were tailored to the family's needs, and affirmed the change of plan to adoption.
key_cases.relevance: Supplies the legal test against which an ordered service plan is measured at each permanency hearing.
key_cases.quote: we conclude that the juvenile court did not err as a matter of law in determining that DHS's efforts were reasonable under ORS 419B.476
